name: Trap Botox (Barbie Botox)

lead: Trap Botox, popularly called Barbie Botox, is botulinum toxin injected into the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the slope from neck to shoulder looks softer and slimmer. It went viral under the Barbie Botox name.

The toxin weakens the injected muscle so it relaxes and loses bulk over time, changing the shoulder-neck line. A 2024 systematic review in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery examined the trend, and trapezius injection is also used in clinical settings such as chronic migraine and cervical dystonia. Detailed cosmetic outcome data for this look are limited.

paras: A clinician injects the trapezius in an office visit, and people repeat treatments as the effect wears off over months. Results build gradually as the muscle relaxes, and it is sometimes mentioned alongside other toxin treatments.
It is an off-label cosmetic use of a prescription product. Neck and shoulder muscle weakness is a general toxin concern, and the effect is temporary.

angle.text: Trap Botox is promoted to relax the trapezius so the neck looks longer and the shoulder line more slender. The toxin weakens the muscle so it loses bulk over time. It is an off-label cosmetic use; a 2024 systematic review covers the trend.

lead: Trap Botox, popularly called Barbie Botox, is the off-label cosmetic injection of botulinum toxin into the trapezius, the broad muscle that runs from the base of the skull across the shoulders. People request it to soften the slope of the neck-to-shoulder line and make the neck look longer and slimmer, an effect often compared with the elongated neck of dolls and fashion imagery.[1]

The route to that look is muscle relaxation. Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, so the injected muscle contracts less; with reduced activity and bulk in the upper trapezius, the shoulder line can appear lower and the neck more visible.[2]

A 2024 systematic review in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery covers the trend, and registered clinical trials involve toxin injection in neck muscles for cervical dystonia, migraine and radiation-related neck contractures; no trial of trapezius toxin for neck appearance itself has been identified.[1][3][4][5]
infobox: About two to four months (facial use)

paras: The procedure aims to reduce trapezius bulk using a neuromodulator so the neck-shoulder line looks elongated.[1] The trapezius is a large, paired, flat muscle running from the occipital bone and nuchal ligament down the thoracic spine and out to the scapula and clavicle. Its upper fibres raise the shoulder blade, the middle fibres pull it toward the spine and the lower fibres depress and rotate it; the accessory nerve supplies its motor control.[6]
Because the upper fibres elevate the shoulder, a stronger or bulkier upper trapezius can make the neck look shorter, and this is the muscle practitioners say the injections target.

The toxin, produced by Clostridium botulinum, cleaves SNARE proteins in nerve terminals and blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing a temporary flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle.[2] For facial cosmetic uses, smoothing is usually visible three to five days after injection, peaks about a week later and typically lasts two to four months, after which muscles can be retreated; some products last six months or longer.[2]
Continued high doses can cause muscles to atrophy or lose strength, which research indicates recovers after a break from treatment.[2]

Coverage of the trend in 2023 quotes plastic surgeons and others describing the treatment. Barry Weintraub, a Manhattan plastic surgeon and American Society of Plastic Surgeons spokesperson, told Fox News Digital that the injection stops the trapezius from contracting and so slims the neck, with results appearing four or five days later and no downtime; he said his office charges about $2,000 because covering so large a muscle takes "a lot of Botox".[7]

In a PureWow explainer, plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine described the treatment as a neuromodulator injected into the trapezius between the neck and shoulders, and plastic surgeon Ron Espinoza said it weakens the muscle and that repeated treatments can cause atrophy, which may make the neck look longer; Espinoza said effects usually last three to four months and that the injections could weaken shoulder and arm movements.[8] Levine said it is not advisable for people with neuromuscular disorders, that people with autoimmune muscle conditions should tell their doctor, and that a skilled provider should examine the patient first to confirm the tension arises from the trapezius.[8] The same article notes that some people seek it for headache relief because weaker neck muscles may reduce headache frequency.[8]

Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin began with a 1989 case report by Richard Clark on forehead wrinkles and the 1992 report by J.D. and J.A. Carruthers of improvement in frown lines, with 16 of 17 participants with follow-up improving. The FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002.[2] The FDA approved Botox for prophylaxis of chronic migraine on 15 October 2010, a use that involves injection sites in the neck and shoulder muscles.[2] The term Barbie Botox for trapezius injection spread on social media and was the subject of a 2024 systematic review of the trend.[1]

Registered trials of toxin in neck muscles address medical conditions. One trial of injection-site strategies in cervical dystonia lists the trapezius among seven muscle groups,[3] a companion study addresses chronic migraine,[4] and a 2011 trial enrolled 14 people with neck contractures after radiosurgery.[5] Additional registered studies cover muscle stiffness and tenderness in chronic migraine patients across a treatment cycle, and toxin for new daily persistent headache.[9][10]

For botulinum toxin in general, Wikipedia lists unintended muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, headaches, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions, and notes that the toxin can spread from the injection site. The FDA issued warnings about spread in 2008 and added boxed warnings in 2009.[2] Specific adverse-event data for cosmetic trapezius injection were not found; neck and shoulder weakness is a general concern for toxin near these muscles.

The procedure is off-label: the FDA-approved cosmetic indication is for frown lines, and prescribers may use toxin for other purposes, which is common.[2] The trend is discussed on social media and in the 2024 systematic review under the Barbie Botox name.[1]

No studies found of trapezius toxin for cosmetic neck appearance beyond the 2024 published systematic review of the trend, which is a review rather than a trial.[1] Registered trials involving trapezius injection address cervical dystonia and migraine.[3][4]
The 2024 systematic review of the trend appears in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery; no controlled trial of cosmetic trapezius injection has been identified.[1]

timeline.event: Richard Clark reports botulinum toxin for forehead wrinkles.[2]
Carruthers and Carruthers report improvement in frown lines.[2]
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for frown lines.[2]
FDA announces boxed warnings about toxin spread.[2]
Botulinum toxin is FDA-approved for chronic migraine.[2]
Systematic review of the Barbie Botox trend is published in JPRAS.[1]
